title: Where Does the Surplus Go? A Mass-Balance Commentary on the Energetics of Muscle Accretion
content: A recent paper by Nikolaidis and colleagues provides the first bottom-up calculation of the energetic cost of building 1 kg of wet human skeletal muscle, estimating a central value of 14,570 kJ/kg (3,481 kcal/kg). The paper's most striking finding is that common applied surpluses of 300–500 kcal/day are nearly tenfold higher than the calculated tissue-specific requirement. This commentary accepts the paper's calculation as a valuable reference point and asks two questions that the paper leaves open: (1) What determines the protein deposition efficiency, and (2) Where does the surplus go? The mass-balance framework suggests that protein deposition efficiency is not a free parameter but a consequence of myonuclear capacity, which scales with surface area. And the surplus does not disappear – it goes to fat mass, because muscle accretion is geometrically constrained while fat accretion is not. The commentary proposes a two-panel figure to illustrate both points. The framework is not a critique of the paper; it is a refinement that connects the calculation to the geometry of tissue accretion.
